The speckled pavon (Cichla temensis) reaches an ultimate total length of 99 centimeters [Li = 99 centimeters] according to published accounts, although some field measurements indicate a somewhat shorter maximum dimension. This large-bodied neotropical cichlid is apex predator in the blackwater and clearwater rivers of the Amazon basin, where it preys on smaller fish and crustaceans. During the breeding season, females produce adhesive eggs deposited in prepared nests guarded by both parents. The wet weight at birth for newly hatched larvae is approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams], reflecting the modest egg diameter of about 2 millimeters from which these yolk-dependent larvae emerge. At a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the onset of exogenous feeding occurs at 2.5 days [ab = 2.5 days] after fertilization, a rapid developmental pace typical of many tropical cichlids with extended parental care. This brief incubation period contrasts sharply with temperate species, where cooler temperatures can prolong embryogenesis considerably.

Female speckled pavon attain sexual maturation at a total length of 33.5 centimeters [Lp = 33.5 centimeters], corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of 564.8 grams [Wwp = 564.8 grams] as derived from length-weight regressions for this species. The onset of gonadal development is closely tied to seasonal flood pulses, which provide abundant foraging habitat and spawning substrates. Males typically mature at slightly smaller sizes, though the precise dimorphism in maturation length has not been systematically quantified across the species' extensive range. Once reproductively active, females produce approximately 1370 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1370 eggs per spawning event] and can complete up to two spawning events per year [F_R_i = up to two spawning events per year] under favorable hydrological conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], which translates to a daily reproduction rate of approximately 2,740 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 2,740 eggs per year]. This reproductive output is moderate compared to other large cichlids, reflecting the energetic investment in nest guarding and brood care that characterizes the genus Cichla.

The maximum recorded lifespan for speckled pavon in natural systems is approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years], based on otolith readings from individuals collected across multiple Amazonian tributaries at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Older individuals become increasingly rare in populations subjected to fishing pressure, as this species is highly prized by both subsistence and sport anglers throughout its distribution. Growth increments slow markedly after the third year, with individuals approaching asymptotic body dimensions thereafter. The ultimate wet weight attained by adult speckled pavon reaches up to 15,700 grams [Wwi = up to 15,700 grams] in the largest documented specimens, though more commonly reported maxima in exploited populations fall closer to 12 kilograms. This body mass is among the highest recorded for any member of the Cichlidae, placing Cichla temensis among the true giants of its family, comparable in size to the largest African cichlids of the genus Boulengerochromis.

Juvenile speckled pavon undergo a distinct trophic shift as they grow, transitioning from zooplanktivory to piscivory once they reach approximately 10 to 15 centimeters in total length. This dietary transition supports rapid somatic growth during the first year, when individuals can more than double their initial mass within weeks of first exogenous feeding. The phase of rapid mass increase is critical for survival, as smaller juveniles face intense predation from larger conspecifics and other piscivorous fishes inhabiting the same floodplain environments. Habitat complexity provided by submerged woody debris and flooded vegetation offers essential refuge during this vulnerable period. Comparative studies with congeneric species such as Cichla ocellaris indicate that the speckled pavon exhibits a somewhat slower juvenile growth trajectory, possibly reflecting its occupation of more nutrient-poor blackwater habitats where prey densities are lower and metabolic demands are shaped by the warmer thermal regime typical of these equatorial waters.

Field observations indicate that the speckled pavon demonstrates pronounced site fidelity to specific spawning grounds, often returning to the same root masses or submerged tree trunks in consecutive breeding seasons. Males establish and defend nesting territories with considerable aggression, while females evaluate nest quality before depositing their clutch. Seasonal reproductive activity peaks during the rising water period when dissolved oxygen levels are highest and newly inundated floodplains provide optimal nursery habitat for the pelagic, yolk-dependent larvae. Parental guarding continues for several weeks following hatching, with both adults aggressively defending the brood against potential predators, including other cichlids and characins. The combination of large body size, territorial behavior, and extended brood care makes Cichla temensis a dominant resident of the Amazonian fish community, structuring prey populations through its predatory pressure and influencing the spatial distribution of smaller fish species within its preferred habitats across the lowland river systems it inhabits.
